From: Harbourglass Ventures Pty Ltd (Seller) counsel
To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)
Re: Project Kestrel - Share Purchase Agreement, Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter

Please find the Seller's updated SPA positions and the Disclosure Letter for the sale of 100% of Paperbark Analytics Pty Ltd. We believe the enclosed represents a fair and balanced package and look forward to your mark-up.

SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)

Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.

Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the basket is recoverable.

Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise.

Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.

Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.

Disclosure (Schedule 7): The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public registers (see Disclosure Letter).

Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records.

Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent.

Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding) will be addressed by a release to be provided following Completion.

Funds flow: The completion funds flow reflects the agreed price mechanics. (The DD-005 closing bonuses of AUD 420,000 are a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised in the funds flow.)

Clause 11.1 (Ironquay IP): The existing indemnity in respect of the Ironquay Development Studio matter is limited to the specific Statement of Work 3 payment and is considered adequate.

Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (Incident): The DD-006 export matter is a preliminary operational matter and is not expected to be material.

Supplier renewals: The three Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate) are ordinary-course operating costs.

Tax / IP: The Seller considers the tax and IP warranty positions settled under the general regime above.

Title: Title to 100% of the shares is evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012.

Project Kestrel - Seller Disclosure Letter (SPA-003). All entities, people, transactions and records are fictional.

1. General Disclosures
[1.1] The Seller discloses every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including DD-002 to DD-012.
[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent, payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required.

3. Riverlark: DD-003 records ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding with change-control 8.1 and discharge 9.2. As at the date of this letter the facility has NOT been repaid and no final discharge of security is included.

4. Ironquay: DD-004 clause 7.3 conditions transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 records AUD 180,000 open; this is not independent bank verification of non-payment. No receipt of payment or confirmatory assignment is in the data room.

## Overall assessment

The package is materially Seller-favourable. The principal concerns are:

1. Bluefen consent and Riverlark discharge are not secured before Completion.
2. Known liabilities are being left in the Company despite the debt-free/cash-free deal.
3. The Seller is attempting to disclose the entire data room and public record wholesale.
4. Liability limitations are extended far beyond ordinary warranty claims.
5. Fundamental title, tax and core IP protections are inadequate.
6. Several known matters require specific remediation or indemnities, rather than mere disclosure.

Our review is necessarily subject to the actual SPA, disclosure bundle and funds flow, which should be marked up directly.

## Detailed issues and recommended pushback

### 1. Bluefen consent — make this a genuine condition precedent

Bluefen represents approximately 30% of FY26 revenue. The current proposal only requires “reasonable endeavours” and treats the condition as satisfied upon delivery of a written consent, even though:

- no final consent has been provided;
- clause 11.3 apparently imposes additional conditions; and
- the consent could contain adverse commercial conditions, fees, price changes or termination rights.

**Push back for:**

- Completion conditional on receipt of final, unconditional and irrevocable written consent in form and substance satisfactory to the Buyer.
- Evidence that every condition under clauses 11.2 and 11.3 has been satisfied or validly waived.
- No amendment, fee, concession or other adverse term without Buyer approval.
- Seller responsibility for consent fees and pre-Completion compliance failures.
- A Buyer termination right if the condition is not satisfied by the long-stop date.
- A bring-down confirmation at Completion that Bluefen has not terminated, threatened termination or materially reduced its business.

This should not be deemed satisfied merely because a document labelled “consent” is delivered.

### 2. Riverlark debt and security — discharge must occur at Completion

A post-Completion release is inconsistent with a debt-free/cash-free acquisition. It could leave the acquired Company liable for AUD 3.2 million and its assets subject to Riverlark security after ownership transfers.

**Push back for:**

- A current payout letter before Completion.
- Repayment directly from Seller’s Completion proceeds, not from the Company or Buyer.
- Simultaneous, unconditional release of the Company and all guarantees and security at Completion.
- PPSR discharge undertakings and evidence of registration discharge promptly after Completion.
- The debt, interest, break costs and discharge expenses treated as indebtedness and deducted from the purchase price.
- Completion not occurring unless the release mechanics are irrevocably in place.

A promise to provide the release “following Completion” is inadequate.

### 3. Completion bonuses — Seller liability and purchase-price deduction

The AUD 420,000 bonuses are triggered by Completion and are omitted from funds flow. Economically, they arise from the Seller’s transaction and should not reduce the value delivered to the Buyer.

The exposure may exceed AUD 420,000 once superannuation, payroll tax, workers compensation premiums and other on-costs are included.

**Push back for:**

- All bonuses and on-costs paid by the Seller or deducted from Completion consideration.
- The amounts included expressly within “Indebtedness”, “Transaction Costs” or an equivalent price-adjustment category.
- No payment from Company cash unless that cash is correspondingly credited to the Buyer.
- A specific indemnity for all bonus-related liabilities, taxes and employee claims.
- Confirmation of the recipients, contractual terms, calculations and applicable on-costs.

Characterising this as “a matter for the Seller” is not enough unless the funds flow actually gives effect to that position.

### 4. General disclosure — reject the data-room dump

Disclosure of every fact “contained or referred to” anywhere in the data room and in publicly searchable records is excessively broad. It transfers to the Buyer the risk of finding and interpreting fragmented or obscure information.

Disclosure should qualify warranties only where it is **fairly disclosed with sufficient detail to identify the nature and reasonably foreseeable scope of the matter**.

**Push back for:**

- Delete general disclosure of the entire data room and public registers.
- Require specific disclosure against identified warranties.
- At minimum, impose a robust fair-disclosure standard and require precise document references.
- Public records should qualify warranties only if expressly identified and fairly summarised.
- Fix a complete, indexed and downloadable data-room snapshot to the Disclosure Letter.
- Require disclosure updates through Completion, but no new disclosure should qualify warranties without Buyer acceptance.
- Preserve claims where information is incomplete, misleading, internally inconsistent or merely invites further inquiry.

The disclosure cutoff of **22 September 2026** is also stale relative to the current transaction timetable. The Seller should provide an updated disclosure letter and Completion bring-down.

### 5. Buyer knowledge — delete constructive and adviser knowledge

The proposed knowledge exclusion captures matters:

- known by any Buyer adviser;
- discoverable from the data room; or
- discoverable from public records.

This effectively turns the warranties into a due-diligence test and substantially neutralises their risk-allocation purpose.

**Push back for:**

- Preferably delete the Buyer-knowledge exclusion.
- Otherwise restrict it to actual, conscious knowledge of a short list of named senior Buyer deal-team members at signing.
- Exclude constructive, imputed and adviser knowledge.
- State expressly that the Buyer has no duty to investigate.
- Place the burden of proving knowledge on the Seller.
- Preserve claims for fraud, deliberate concealment, misleading conduct, specific indemnities, title and tax matters.

### 6. Liability cap — 20% is Seller-favourable

A 20% cap may be within the range seen in some transactions, particularly with warranty insurance, but it is low for an uninsured transaction with the identified gaps and known issues.

**Push back for:**

- A higher general warranty cap—ideally 50%, with 30% as a potential negotiated fallback depending on diligence and security.
- Separate caps for distinct protection categories.
- Fundamental/title claims capped at 100% of the purchase price.
- Tax claims and specific indemnities capped at 100% or the relevant liability amount.
- No cap for fraud, wilful misconduct, deliberate concealment, leakage, unpaid indebtedness, purchase-price adjustments or breach of Completion obligations.

Any cap should apply to the Seller’s liability, not reduce recovery for amounts received from third parties only hypothetically or before they are actually recovered.

### 7. Thresholds — limit them to general warranty claims

AUD 25,000 is approximately 0.10% of the price, and the AUD 250,000 basket is approximately 1.04%. The amounts are not extraordinary, but the “excess only” basket is Seller-favourable.

**Push back for:**

- A tipping basket: once the basket is exceeded, recovery begins from the first dollar.
- Alternatively, reduce the deductible basket.
- Aggregate related claims for the de minimis threshold.
- Apply thresholds only to general warranty claims.
- Exclude title, capacity, tax, specific indemnities, leakage, indebtedness, price-adjustment claims, covenants and fraud.

### 8. Time limits — 18 months should not apply universally

An 18-month limitation may be negotiable for general business warranties, but it is inappropriate for title, tax, known risks and contractual obligations.

**Push back for:**

- General warranties: at least 24 months, preferably 24–36 months.
- Tax: seven years after Completion or the applicable statutory review period plus a buffer.
- Fundamental/title/capacity claims: six years or the applicable statutory limitation period.
- Specific indemnities: tailored periods ending after the relevant exposure has been finally resolved.
- Fraud and deliberate concealment: no contractual time bar.
- Timely notification should preserve a claim; immaterial defects in notice should not invalidate it unless the Seller is materially prejudiced.
- Permit notification of contingent, unquantified and third-party claims.

### 9. “All Claims” limitations and exclusive remedy — reject

Applying caps, thresholds, time limits, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions to **all claims of any nature** is much broader than limiting warranty claims. It could capture:

- specific indemnities;
- Completion covenants;
- debt and price adjustments;
- leakage;
- tax covenants;
- fraud or deliberate concealment;
- misleading or deceptive conduct;
- equitable remedies; and
- post-Completion obligations.

**Push back for express carve-outs** covering all of the above. Any exclusive-remedy provision should apply only to ordinary warranty claims, and should preserve statutory rights that cannot lawfully be excluded, including applicable Australian Consumer Law remedies.

### 10. Fundamental title and capacity — require full protection

The share register is evidence, but not conclusive protection against competing beneficial interests, encumbrances, defective issuances or undisclosed arrangements.

**Push back for:**

- Fundamental warranties covering legal and beneficial ownership, valid issuance, full payment, absence of encumbrances, options and third-party rights, and authority to sell.
- A 100% purchase-price cap and long limitation period.
- No de minimis, basket, Buyer-knowledge or general-disclosure qualification.
- Completion delivery of executed transfers, original share certificates or agreed lost-certificate documents, updated registers and all required corporate approvals.
- PPSR and corporate searches and releases of any security affecting the shares.
- A specific indemnity if any title anomaly is identified.

### 11. Ironquay IP — remediate before Completion

The Company apparently does not receive ownership of SOW3 Project Materials until every fee is paid, and AUD 180,000 remains recorded as open. For an analytics business, uncertainty over core IP ownership is material.

The proposed indemnity limited to the specific unpaid fee does not protect against loss of IP rights, infringement claims, business interruption or remediation costs.

**Push back for:**

- Payment of all SOW3 fees by the Seller before Completion.
- Written confirmation from Ironquay that payment is complete and IP has vested or been validly assigned.
- Delivery of a confirmatory assignment covering all relevant materials and rights.
- Evidence concerning source code, repositories, moral-rights consents and subcontractor assignments.
- A broader specific indemnity for all loss arising from non-payment, deficient ownership, infringement or failure of assignment.
- The indemnity outside the general cap, basket and time limit.

The AUD 180,000 should also be treated as debt or a Seller transaction cost if unpaid at Completion.

### 12. Export/privacy incident — investigation and specific protection required

The matter potentially involves approximately 1,240 individuals. Business emails, roles and activity timestamps may constitute personal information. The current evidence does not establish access, scope, containment or whether the Notifiable Data Breaches regime applies.

“Preliminary” does not mean immaterial.

**Push back for:**

- Immediate forensic investigation by an appropriately qualified adviser.
- Access logs, download evidence, recipient details, containment steps and deletion confirmation.
- A documented legal assessment of Privacy Act, contractual and regulatory notification obligations.
- Prompt notice of any development before Completion.
- No regulator or affected-person communication without Buyer consultation, except where legally required.
- Remediation before Completion where possible.
- A specific indemnity covering investigation, notification, remediation, third-party claims, regulatory action and business interruption arising from the incident.
- No general cap, basket or 18-month limitation for that indemnity.
- A retention or escrow if the exposure remains unresolved at Completion.

### 13. Supplier renewals — reflect their economic substance

Three related AUD 110,000 renewals are material in aggregate. The Seller has not established whether they are terminable, accrued, unavoidable or properly attributable to the post-Completion period.

**Push back for:**

- Copies of the complete agreements, renewal notices and termination terms.
- Confirmation whether the commitments were entered into in the ordinary course and on arm’s-length terms.
- No renewal, prepayment or material amendment before Completion without Buyer consent.
- Accrued or overdue amounts included in working capital or indebtedness as appropriate.
- Pre-Completion service periods borne by the Seller; post-Completion prepaid benefits credited to the Buyer.
- Review for related-party or transaction-driven arrangements.

The Seller cannot establish ordinary-course treatment merely by asserting it.

### 14. Tax protections — require a separate tax covenant

Tax should not sit solely within the 20%/18-month general warranty regime.

**Push back for:**

- A customary tax deed or tax covenant covering all tax attributable to pre-Completion periods and Seller-group arrangements.
- Coverage for payroll tax, superannuation, employee bonuses, GST, withholding and transaction-related liabilities.
- A 100% cap, no basket and a limitation period tied to statutory assessment periods.
- Control provisions for tax claims that protect the Buyer’s ongoing business and reputation.
- No qualification by general disclosure or constructive Buyer knowledge.

### 15. Remaining contract and Completion points

- **Office lease:** confirm the notice requirement, give timely notice and obtain evidence of compliance. Confirm there is no default or termination right arising from the transaction.
- **Mossvale:** an assignment restriction may not apply to a share sale, but the full agreement should be checked for change-of-control, indirect transfer and termination provisions.
- **Interim conduct:** require operation in the ordinary course, preservation of customers and staff, no material commitments or settlements, and prompt incident reporting.
- **Warranty bring-down:** warranties should be repeated at Completion by reference to then-current facts.
- **Price mechanics:** verify that the SPA clearly implements an AUD 24 million debt-free/cash-free price, with robust definitions of cash, indebtedness, transaction costs and normalised working capital. Riverlark debt, bonuses, Ironquay amounts and relevant supplier accruals must not fall through definitional gaps.
- **Security for claims:** consider escrow, retention, guarantee or other recourse, especially if Harbourglass will distribute the proceeds after Completion.

## Recommended negotiating priorities

### Completion blockers

1. Obtain acceptable Bluefen consent and satisfy all associated conditions.
2. Repay Riverlark and release all security simultaneously with Completion.
3. Resolve Ironquay payment and secure confirmatory IP ownership.
4. Allocate bonuses and on-costs to the Seller in the funds flow.
5. Investigate and contain the privacy/export incident.

### Core SPA changes

1. Reject wholesale data-room/public-record disclosure.
2. Delete constructive and adviser knowledge.
3. Limit the general cap, thresholds and 18-month period strictly to general warranty claims.
4. Give title, tax and specific indemnities separate, materially stronger protection.
5. Carve fraud, deliberate concealment, debt, price adjustments, leakage, covenants and Completion obligations out of all general limitations.
6. Require updated disclosure and warranty bring-down at Completion.

The Buyer should not accept the package as drafted. The known issues should be resolved through Completion conditions, price mechanics and specific indemnities—not left to a heavily capped and time-limited general warranty regime.

- Confirmation whether the commitments were entered into in the ordinary course and on arm’s-length terms.
- No renewal, prepayment or material amendment before Completion without Buyer consent.
- Accrued or overdue amounts included in working capital or indebtedness as appropriate.
- Pre-Completion service periods borne by the Seller; post-Completion prepaid benefits credited to the Buyer.
- Review for related-party or transaction-driven arrangements.

The Seller cannot establish ordinary-course treatment merely by asserting it.

### 14. Tax protections — require a separate tax covenant

Tax should not sit solely within the 20%/18-month general warranty regime.

**Push back for:**

- A customary tax deed or tax covenant covering all tax attributable to pre-Completion periods and Seller-group arrangements.
- Coverage for payroll tax, superannuation, employee bonuses, GST, withholding and transaction-related liabilities.
- A 100% cap, no basket and a limitation period tied to statutory assessment periods.
- Control provisions for tax claims that protect the Buyer’s ongoing business and reputation.
- No qualification by general disclosure or constructive Buyer knowledge.

### 15. Remaining contract and Completion points

- **Office lease:** confirm the notice requirement, give timely notice and obtain evidence of compliance. Confirm there is no default or termination right arising from the transaction.
- **Mossvale:** an assignment restriction may not apply to a share sale, but the full agreement should be checked for change-of-control, indirect transfer and termination provisions.
- **Interim conduct:** require operation in the ordinary course, preservation of customers and staff, no material commitments or settlements, and prompt incident reporting.
- **Warranty bring-down:** warranties should be repeated at Completion by reference to then-current facts.
- **Price mechanics:** verify that the SPA clearly implements an AUD 24 million debt-free/cash-free price, with robust definitions of cash, indebtedness, transaction costs and normalised working capital. Riverlark debt, bonuses, Ironquay amounts and relevant supplier accruals must not fall through definitional gaps.
- **Security for claims:** consider escrow, retention, guarantee or other recourse, especially if Harbourglass will distribute the proceeds after Completion.

## Recommended negotiating priorities

### Completion blockers

1. Obtain acceptable Bluefen consent and satisfy all associated conditions.
2. Repay Riverlark and release all security simultaneously with Completion.
3. Resolve Ironquay payment and secure confirmatory IP ownership.
4. Allocate bonuses and on-costs to the Seller in the funds flow.
5. Investigate and contain the privacy/export incident.

### Core SPA changes

1. Reject wholesale data-room/public-record disclosure.
2. Delete constructive and adviser knowledge.
3. Limit the general cap, thresholds and 18-month period strictly to general warranty claims.
4. Give title, tax and specific indemnities separate, materially stronger protection.
5. Carve fraud, deliberate concealment, debt, price adjustments, leakage, covenants and Completion obligations out of all general limitations.
6. Require updated disclosure and warranty bring-down at Completion.

The Buyer should not accept the package as drafted. The known issues should be resolved through Completion conditions, price mechanics and specific indemnities—not left to a heavily capped and time-limited general warranty regime.
